topic.name: Did the United States Contain the Spread of Communism?

subtopics.name: Why Did Communism 'Need' to be Contained?

parts.problem_md:
**The Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953.**

How successful was the USA in the Korean War? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
The USA achieved what it went to Korea to do. Whether that made the war a success depends on what containment was supposed to deliver [R].

The immediate aim was met. North Korea invaded in June 1950 with Soviet and Chinese backing, UN forces under MacArthur landed at Inchon that September and pushed the invasion back, and the armistice left Korea divided at the 38th Parallel [R]. South Korea was protected from communism, so containment worked exactly as intended in the place it was first tested [E].

The USA also won the argument internationally. Truman persuaded the UN Security Council to act, 18 member states provided troops, and the USSR's boycott meant it could not veto the decision [R]. The UN had stood up to aggression in a way the League of Nations never did, which gave American policy a legitimacy that later interventions lacked [E].

However, containment could stop communism but not reverse it. North Korea remained communist and formed closer ties with China [R]. When MacArthur pushed to the Yalu River, Mao sent Chinese forces, Seoul was recaptured and UN troops retreated behind the 38th Parallel; MacArthur then asked for a nuclear attack on China and Truman sacked him for it [R]. The USA ended the war on the line it had started from [A].

The wider consequences were worse. The war caused four million casualties, including 50,000 American dead, and the USA then built anti-communist alliances in SEATO and CENTO which left the USSR feeling surrounded [R]. Both superpowers accelerated a nuclear arms race, developing hydrogen bombs and ICBMs [R]. A war that makes the next confrontation more dangerous has not made the world safer [A].

The Korean War was therefore successful only to a limited extent. Judged narrowly, it was containment's one clear victory, and South Korea exists today because of it [A]. Judged by what the USA actually wanted, a world where communism stopped spreading, it achieved a stalemate at enormous cost and left both sides more heavily armed than before. The USA held the line and called it winning [A].

parts.problem_md:
**American containment was tested in the Caribbean and in South East Asia.**

Which was the greater failure of American containment: Cuba or Vietnam? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Cuba embarrassed the United States. Vietnam destroyed the policy it was fighting for. That difference decides the question [R].

Cuba humiliated the USA at the Bay of Pigs. In April 1961 1,400 CIA-trained exiles landed and surrendered in under 24 hours, because Castro knew they were coming and met them with 20,000 soldiers [R]. The failure damaged the USA's reputation badly: having accused the USSR of forcing Eastern Europe to live under its influence, the USA had attempted an armed uprising against an independent government [E].

Cuba also failed permanently. The island stayed communist and allied to the USSR, Kennedy promised not to invade, and Khrushchev secured the removal of US missiles from Turkey [R]. A communist state survived 90 miles from the American coast for the rest of the Cold War, which is the clearest possible breach of containment [A].

Vietnam, however, cost incomparably more. Around 2.8 million Americans served, over 58,000 died alongside millions of Vietnamese casualties, and the war cost roughly \$168 billion [R]. Chemical warfare and atrocities such as My Lai ruined the USA's international reputation, so the country lost the propaganda argument as well as the war [E].

Vietnam also ended containment itself. The Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 closed US involvement, Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, and by then Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia were all communist, giving the USSR and China new allies [R]. The US government then abandoned containment altogether, with Nixon turning instead to detente [R]. Cuba was a defeat inside the policy; Vietnam was the defeat of the policy [A].

Vietnam was therefore the greater failure. Cuba was a single humiliating operation, and the USA partly recovered from it in October 1962 when the blockade forced Khrushchev to remove the missiles [A]. Vietnam offered no such recovery. It ran for two decades, consumed lives and money on a scale Cuba never approached, and ended with Washington concluding that the strategy it had followed since 1947 no longer worked [A].

parts.problem_md:
**The USA applied containment in Korea, Cuba and Vietnam.**

'The United States failed to contain the spread of communism.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Containment stopped communism wherever the USA could apply pressure at a single point. It failed wherever communism was already popular on the ground [R].

Cuba, initially, showed that containment had failed. The Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961 collapsed within 24 hours, and after the missile crisis Cuba remained communist and allied to the USSR, with Kennedy promising not to invade [R]. Khrushchev also secured the quiet removal of US missiles from Turkey [R]. Containment existed to stop communism spreading, and here it appeared 90 miles from the American coast and stayed [E].

Vietnam was worse. Containment failed militarily, because the Viet Cong had better tactics than a better-armed enemy, and politically, because by 1975 Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia were all communist [R]. It cost around \$168 billion and over 58,000 American lives, and afterwards the US government abandoned containment altogether, Nixon pursuing detente instead [R]. A policy its own government gives up has failed on its own terms [A].

However, Korea worked. North Korea invaded in June 1950, UN forces pushed the invasion back, and the armistice kept Korea divided at the 38th Parallel, so South Korea was protected from communism [R]. The USA also secured international legitimacy that the League of Nations never managed, with 18 member states sending troops [E].

The Cuban Missile Crisis ultimately provided a success for containment. The blockade of October 1962 forced Khrushchev to back down and remove the missile sites, which was a propaganda victory for containment, and Kennedy maintained world peace while doing it [R]. Faced with a threat it could physically intercept, the policy did exactly what it was designed to do [A].

The statement is therefore true to a large extent, but the pattern matters more than the verdict. Where the USA could hold a line or stop a ship, at the 38th Parallel or in the Caribbean, containment worked [A]. Where communism was homegrown and popular, in Cuba after 1959 and across Vietnam, no amount of American money or firepower could remove it. Containment could halt communism; it could never reverse it [A].

parts.problem_md:
**The USA had a huge technological advantage in Vietnam.**

Why did the USA fail to defeat the Vietcong?
parts.solution_md:
One reason was that Viet Cong tactics cancelled out American strength. The Viet Cong knew the USA would win in open warfare, so instead they set traps, ambushed soldiers, used Vietnam's forests to attack and hide, and dug tunnels [R]. They wore no military uniform, and many South Vietnamese citizens helped them, so US soldiers struggled to tell fighters from civilians [R]. This mattered because American advantages in firepower and technology were useless against an enemy who would not stand and fight and who could not reliably be identified [E].

A second reason was that US tactics created more enemies than they removed. Search and Destroy sent troops by helicopter to find Viet Cong bases, but the operations killed innocent villagers, while napalm and Agent Orange caused high civilian casualties [R]. Supplies also kept moving south along the Ho Chi Minh Trail despite constant US bombing [R]. This explains the failure because every operation pushed more Vietnamese towards supporting the Viet Cong, so the USA was generating opposition faster than it could destroy it [E].

parts.problem_md:
**The USA attempted to overthrow Castro in 1961.**

Why did the Bay of Pigs invasion fail?
parts.solution_md:
One reason was that the invasion force was too weak and was deliberately left unsupported. On 17 April 1961 the US government sent 1,400 Cuban exiles to land in the Bay of Pigs, and the CIA had given them only limited military training [R]. To distance itself from the invasion, the US government then refused to send military support [R]. This was decisive because the whole plan depended on the operation looking like a counter-revolution rather than a US invasion, and that same disguise denied the exiles the firepower they needed, so they surrendered in under 24 hours [E].

A second reason was that Castro was both prepared and popular. He knew about the invasion before it began and assembled an army of 20,000 soldiers to meet the exiles as they landed [R]. Cuban citizens were also content with his government, so the invasion attracted very little support on the island [R]. This mattered because the plan assumed the Cuban people would rise up and remove Castro once the exiles arrived; since they would not, no invasion force of that size could have succeeded however well equipped it had been [E].

parts.problem_md:
**North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950.**

Why did the USA get involved in the Korean War?
parts.solution_md:
One reason was that the USA wanted to protect its economic interests in Asia. The Domino Theory held that if Korea fell to communism, its powerful neighbour Japan would be next, and Japan was an important market for US exports which the USA wanted to keep capitalist [R]. Protecting South Korea was therefore a way of protecting the wider trading system the USA had built across the Pacific, since a communist takeover in Korea threatened to spread further and close markets that had previously been open to American goods [R]. This mattered because Korea's fall would not have stayed a local defeat: it risked costing the USA its most valuable Asian trading partner and, with it, a large part of America's economic position in the whole region [E].

A second reason was that Truman had already committed himself publicly. In 1947 the Truman Doctrine declared that the USA would protect any country under threat of a communist uprising, and the US public now put pressure on the government to protect South Korea [R]. The government also believed it could win, expecting China not to react and hoping to persuade the UN to provide military support [R]. This explains the intervention because North Korea's invasion in June 1950 was the first open communist attack since the doctrine was announced, and ignoring it would have made the whole policy of containment look worthless [E].

parts.problem_md:
**The last US troops left Vietnam in the 1970s.**

Describe the consequences of the Vietnam War for the USA.
parts.solution_md:
Containment had failed militarily, because although the USA had stronger weapons the Viet Cong had better tactics [1]. It had failed politically, because by 1975 Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia had all become communist, giving the USSR and China new allies [1]. It had failed economically, since the war cost the USA around \$168 billion, and over 58,000 US soldiers died [1]. The use of chemical warfare and the disregard for Vietnamese civilians ruined the USA's international reputation, and the US government abandoned containment, with Nixon pursuing detente instead [1].

parts.problem_md:
**In October 1962 the world came close to nuclear war.**

What happened during the 'Thirteen Days' of October 1962?
parts.solution_md:
The Thirteen Days ran from 16 to 28 October 1962, and were the closest the world had come to nuclear war [1]. On 16 October Kennedy assembled his advisory group ExComm, and on 22 October he told the American public he was imposing a blockade of Cuba [1]. Khrushchev announced on 23 October that Soviet ships would not stop at the blockade, but on 24 October twenty of them turned around [1]. Khrushchev then sent two letters, the second demanding the removal of US missiles in Turkey, and on 28 October Bobby Kennedy and the Soviet ambassador agreed a deal [1].

parts.problem_md:
**Korea was divided at the end of the Second World War.**

Describe how Korea was divided in 1945.
parts.solution_md:
In 1905 Japan had owned Korea, and when Japan surrendered to the Allies in 1945 the terms of that surrender included the division of Korea [1]. Soviet troops were already in the north and US troops in the south, so the Allies split the country into two equal zones along the 38th Parallel [1]. Historians believe Korea was divided in this way to prevent the USSR from taking the whole country [1]. The USSR then monitored North Korea and the USA oversaw South Korea, and each chose an unelected leader: Kim Il Sung in the north and Syngman Rhee in the south [1].

> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the Korean War of 1950-53 instead of the division of 1945.
> - Confusing the 38th Parallel in Korea with the 17th Parallel, which divided Vietnam in 1954.
> - Explaining why the division caused war rather than describing how it happened.
> - Developing two points at length instead of making four separate ones, which caps the mark at 2.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> Answers may include the following. This list is not exhaustive and any other valid point should be credited.
> 
> - The division was intended to be temporary.
> - Both Kim Il Sung and Syngman Rhee claimed to be the legitimate leader of the whole of Korea.
> - Rhee was corrupt and unpopular, and in April 1950 many South Koreans voted in favour of reuniting the country.
> - Many Koreans wanted reunification under the communist Kim Il Sung, which is part of why the division did not hold.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Four separate facts is the target: why Korea needed dividing, where the line was drawn, why that line was chosen, and who ended up in charge of each half.
> - Naming the 38th Parallel and both leaders is precise detail that is quickly credited.
> - Make four distinct points rather than developing two in detail. Extra detail on a point you have already made will not gain you a further mark.
> - No introduction or conclusion is needed, and no extra marks are available beyond four points.

parts.problem_md:
![Source A](assets/001-source-a.png)

![Source B](assets/002-source-b.png)

Study Sources D and E. How far does Source E prove that Taylor’s findings (Source D) were wrong? Explain your answer using details of the sources and your knowledge.
parts.solution_md:
Both sources agree that the Bay of Pigs was a disastrous episode. However, their big messages contradict each other. Source A holds the CIA responsible for the debacle because of its 'weaknesses' and flawed planning, which became more and more 'apparent' as the operation progressed. Source B, in contrast, says it was mainly Kennedy's fault, because he wanted to bring down Castro without spending too much on the mission or being 'visible', which left the attack too weak to achieve anything [S].

Both sources agree on the cancellation of the second air strike. Source A says the 'second air strike was cancelled' by Kennedy, so the invaders received no reinforcement and could do little damage, 'leaving most of Castro's air force intact' [S]. Source B also states that Kennedy 'refused to give air force support'. Secondly, both agree that the USA tried to hide its involvement. Source A notes that the US bombers were 'painted as such that they looked like Cuban air force planes', and that Kennedy cancelled the second strike to show the USA had nothing to do with it. Source B supports this, saying the USA wanted 'minimum visibility' [S].

The sources disagree on more than they agree. Firstly, Source A mainly blames the CIA, which failed to 'keep the secret secure', chose a 'poor site for invasion' and used 'obsolete bombers'. In that account Kennedy is only partly responsible, because he cancelled the second air strike [R]. Source B pins the main responsibility on Kennedy, citing his indecision, the 'cancellation of the second strike' and his 'refusal to give air support'. Secondly, Source A highlights the inefficiency of the bombers, which 'missed many targets', so most of Castro's air force survived. Source B, by contrast, records some success for the raid, after which 'Cuba was left with only eight planes and seven pilots' [S].

To conclude, the two sources partly agree that cancelling the second air strike contributed to the failure, and that the USA did not want to be seen playing any part in the invasion. But they disagree on far more, including the CIA's planning, the casualties and how far Kennedy was responsible for the choices that were made [R].

**[7 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Source analysis - [S]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **7 marks:** a clear, summative, overall judgement comparing the big messages of the two sources. It must be supported; an isolated point of comparison is treated as a single disagreement.
> - **5-6 marks:** compares agreement(s) AND disagreement(s).
> - **3-4 marks:** compares agreement(s) OR disagreement(s), but not both.
> - **2 marks:** answers based on information in one source that is not in the other, or comparing the provenance or topic of the sources.
> - **1 mark:** attempts to compare but makes no valid comparison.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 7 marks include:
> 
> - Focusing on either the agreements or the disagreements and not both.
> - Using your own knowledge, or information that is not in the sources, such as Kennedy's dealings with the CIA.
> - Not quoting the sources accurately, or forgetting to quote them at all.
> - Paraphrasing in a way that changes the meaning of the big messages.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Both sources also agree that the invasion force was trapped, that two ships were sunk and that a large number of soldiers were imprisoned. They disagree on the numbers: Source A says 1,200 invaders were captured and more than 100 killed, while Source B gives 1,197 and 67.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Use both sources to show agreements and disagreements.
> - Keep quotations short and relevant. A few words in quotation marks is enough.
> - Use separate paragraphs for agreement and disagreement.
> - Aim your conclusion at the big messages of the two sources, since that is what reaches 7 marks.

parts.problem_md:
A cartoon published in an American newspaper, 21 April 1961

![Source C](assets/003-source-c.png)

Study Source C. What is the message of this source? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge.
parts.solution_md:
Source C is a political cartoon published in April 1961, after the failure at the Bay of Pigs [R]. Its message is that the invasion was a hopeless failure and that Kennedy's claim to free Cuba remained an unfulfilled promise. The cartoon brings out the weakness of the invasion and establishes Castro's strength [S].

It suggests the invasion was weak, shown by the zig-zag line across the sea, and that Castro defeated it easily. The invasion effort does not even reach the fort, which shows its inherent weakness and quick collapse. Castro is shown well prepared, guarding the fort [S]. He holds a gun, symbolising a well-armed Cuba, and he watches the invasion, which shows he knew it was coming and had taken up his position well in advance. The Cuban fortress is drawn as a strong structure, safe from any damage. The weak planning of the invasion failed, and the fort remained intact [S].

Communist support for Cuba is represented by the Soviet tanks carrying the hammer and sickle [R]. The protection the Soviet Union provided kept Cuba safe from invasion across the water, and this emphasises the alliance between Cuba and the USSR [S].

The central message is that Cuba's 'Liberty' remained trapped inside the fortress and that the American claim to free it went unfulfilled. The caption, 'The Cuban people have not yet spoken their final piece', a statement by President Kennedy, is used ironically: it proved far too optimistic [R].

**[8 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Source analysis - [S]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **8 marks:** gives the big message AND explains the cartoonist's opinion or point of view. An unsupported opinion drops to 5 marks.
> - **6-7 marks:** explains the big message. If the message is stated but not explained, place the answer at 5 marks.
> - **5 marks:** reaches the big message or the cartoonist's opinion but without support from the source.
> - **2-4 marks:** explains valid sub-messages. Only 2 marks where the answer is limited to incidental details.
> - **1 mark:** surface description of the cartoon, or a plausible misinterpretation.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 8 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the drawing or quoting the caption without placing it in its historical context.
> - Not explaining the big message of the source.
> - Naming the symbols without connecting them to the point the cartoonist is making.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The cartoon is an ironic comment on Kennedy's promise to liberate Cuba from a communist regime.
> - It suggests the US government underestimated Castro's strength.
> - The invasion effort is drawn as a zig-zag line, like lightning in an evening sky. It offered a moment of hope that Cuba might be liberated, but the sky stays dark, showing that communism in Cuba remained strong.
> - The Soviet tank protecting the Cuban fortress symbolises the closeness of Cuba and the USSR.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Pay attention to the symbols in the cartoon and say what each one stands for.
> - Identify the message first, then explain the cartoonist's opinion about it. That second step is what reaches the top mark.
> - Use the caption and the provenance to work out the context in which the cartoon was drawn.
> - Avoid long descriptions of what the picture shows.

parts.problem_md: Study all the [sources](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2025/09/55159_June%202024-Source%20File%20-%20converted.pdf). How far do these sources provide convincing evidence that President Kennedy was to blame for the failure of the Bay of Pigs invasion? Use the sources to explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
The sources provide differing views on Kennedy's responsibility for the failure of the Bay of Pigs invasion. Sources B and E support the claim, while C, D and F point the other way. Source A provides both perspectives. Overall, Kennedy had a substantial but not a sole role in the failure: poor CIA planning and Castro's strength were equally responsible for the outcome [R].

Source A says Kennedy cancelled the second air strike to hide US involvement, so the Cuban air force 'remained intact' and 'Castro could control the skies' before attacking the invaders. Source B blames Kennedy for the debacle, saying he was indecisive and 'cancelled the second air strike' [S]. He also refused air support so that the American role stayed at 'minimum visibility'. Similarly, in Source E a CIA historian blames Kennedy's 'actions, or inactions' as the main cause of failure. That source also criticises the Taylor Committee report for protecting the President by 'not interviewing some key witnesses'. Source F shows Kennedy trying to shift responsibility by painting the invasion as a fight of 'Cuban patriots' against 'a Cuban dictator', doing his best to protect his own reputation [S].

On the other hand, Source A stresses that the CIA chose 'a poor site for landing, a swampy area' that was unsuitable. It also failed to keep the plan secret and used 'outdated bombers', which made the first air strike ineffective. Source A adds that Castro knew the strike was coming and stood ready with 20,000 troops [R]. On that reading the invasion was doomed from the start, whatever Kennedy decided. The Taylor Committee report in Source D likewise argues that the CIA's poor organisation and planning were the main cause, and that the operation would have succeeded had it been 'better conceived, better organised, better staffed and better managed', without any need to escalate the issue to the President. Source E, though critical of Kennedy, admits the CIA will always be blamed [S].

To conclude, the sources suggest Kennedy should not be blamed alone, because the CIA was also incompetent. He can be blamed for cancelling the air strikes and for trying to conceal US involvement. But the sources also show that the CIA failed to plan properly or in time. Taken together, Kennedy shared a large but not the sole responsibility for the disaster [S].

**[9 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Source analysis - [S]
> 
> Source use must be referenced by source letter, provenance or a quote. There must be use of source content and an explanation of how this supports or does not support the statement.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **6-9 marks:** uses the sources to support AND to reject the statement. Six marks for one source explained on each side, with further marks within the range for each additional source explained.
> - **3-5 marks:** uses the sources to support OR to reject the statement, but not both.
> - **2 marks:** uses the sources but does not use them to test the statement.
> - **1 mark:** writes about the topic without using the sources.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
> 
> Supporting: B, E, F. Not supporting: C, D. Source A may be credited on both sides.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 6-9 marks include:
> 
> - Taking a source at face value without weighing the whole picture.
> - Not analysing a source for its value and its limitations.
> - Failing to use all of the sources.
> - Using the sources on one side only, which caps the answer at 5 marks.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Consider reliability before accepting a source. Source D blamed the CIA and protected the President, and the committee that produced it was appointed by the President himself.
> - Robert Kennedy, the President's brother, sat on that committee, which raises the possibility of bias.
> - Source E, written by a CIA historian decades later, is arguably more convincing because it was written under less political pressure.
> - Source A comes from a modern history book and gives a balanced account, recognising Kennedy's role while also emphasising CIA errors and Castro's strength.
> - Source F, Kennedy's own speech, was a deliberate attempt to protect his public image, which makes it less reliable as evidence of what happened.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Use all of the sources. Nine marks rewards range, and leaving one out is leaving marks behind.
> - Sort the sources into two groups before you write. You must use both sides.
> - Quoting and summarising is not enough; evaluate each source in the context of the question.
> - Back up your judgement with contextual knowledge, and finish with a clear, concise conclusion.

parts.problem_md:
![Source F](assets/004-source-f.png)

Study Source F. Why did Kennedy make this speech on 20 April 1961? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge.
parts.solution_md:
Kennedy made this speech on 20 April 1961, after the failed Bay of Pigs invasion, to limit the political damage and to convince the American public that the situation was under control. He also wanted to defend the reputation of the United States at a moment when the Cold War was intensifying [R].

According to Kennedy, the invasion was 'a struggle of Cuban patriots against a Cuban dictator'. This supported the idea that the action was not unjustified but an attempt to restore order in Cuba, where Castro was consolidating his power [S].

He also insisted that 'the armed forces of this country would not intervene in any way', which was meant to show that the United States was not responsible for the disaster. In reality the CIA had organised and trained the invaders and supplied their equipment with the approval of the US government. Kennedy wanted to protect the image of the USA as a peaceful nation, so presenting the invasion as a fight led by Cubans themselves was the safer position [S].

Kennedy also did not want to admit that the USA had broken international law by trying to overthrow the government of another country. The speech was an opportunity to portray the conflict as part of a larger struggle of 'liberty against tyranny' [S]. By drawing attention to 'communist tanks' crushing 'freedom fighters', he wanted Americans to focus on the communist threat. This was a way of uniting them behind the idea of the USA as leader of the free world, and of drawing attention away from the American failure at the Bay of Pigs [R].

In conclusion, Kennedy made this speech to influence public opinion after the failure. He wanted to protect his political and personal reputation, conceal the American role in the attack, and present the invasion as part of a worldwide struggle against communism rather than an operation backed by the USA. In the wider Cold War context, with American prestige at stake, the speech was an exercise in damage control [R].

**[8 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Source analysis - [S]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **8 marks:** explains the speaker's purpose in the correct specific context, namely the days immediately after the failed invasion of April 1961.
> - **6-7 marks:** explains the big message of the speaker, properly explained rather than copied from the source.
> - **5 marks:** gives the specific context only, without turning it into a purpose.
> - **2-4 marks:** explains valid sub-messages, or gives only generalised context, or states a purpose without the specific context.
> - **1 mark:** makes points from the levels above but does not use them as reasons for the speech, or gives invalid reasons.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 8 marks include:
> 
> - Taking the speech at face value and ignoring its historical context. Keep asking why the speech was made on 20 April 1961 in particular, rather than before or after.
> - Summarising what Kennedy said. Summary is not the same as explaining why he said it.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Kennedy declared that as president of a democracy he owed the people the truth, yet he carefully avoided any detail of US involvement, which shows how much he needed to protect his reputation after a humiliating defeat.
> - He also wanted to reassure the press and the public that his government remained committed to defending democracy abroad.
> - The speech was made to a group of newspaper editors, which shows he was trying to influence the press and shape opinion in his favour.
> - The Bay of Pigs had made the USA look weak and incompetent, which is why Kennedy focused on Castro's 'communist tanks' crushing freedom fighters, shifting attention from the defeat to the global threat of communism.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Keep asking 'why now?' rather than 'what does it say?'. The date in the question is doing the work.
> - Quote from the source and explain what the wording reveals about Kennedy's motives.
> - Set the speech in the Cold War context: what was at stake for American prestige, and what was Kennedy leaving out?
> - Try to give more than one purpose, since an answer built on several reads far more securely than one built on a single idea.

parts.problem_md:
In October 1962 the world came close to nuclear war.

How far was Castro responsible for the Cuban Missile Crisis? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Castro carries real responsibility [R]. He overthrew Batista in January 1959 and then took the decisions that brought Soviet weapons to an island ninety miles from the American coast. In February 1960 his government signed an agreement with the Soviet Union under which Khrushchev would buy Cuban sugar and, secretly, Cuba would receive Soviet arms. He appointed communists to his government and nationalised land owned by foreign nationals despite American objections. After the Bay of Pigs he publicly announced that he was a communist and asked the USSR to help defend Cuba, and in September 1961 Khrushchev declared that the Soviet Union would supply weapons. Without those invitations there would have been no Soviet missiles on Cuba to discover [E].

Against that, American policy drove him towards Moscow [R]. The United States had propped up Batista for years because US businesses profited from his corrupt rule, and it owned Cuba's oil refineries, railways and electricity alongside its sugar trade. When Castro tried to end that control, Eisenhower cut sugar purchases in July 1960, imposed a trade embargo by October and broke off diplomatic relations by 1961. A country whose main export market has been closed has to find another buyer, and the USSR was the obvious one. The Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961 then turned a trade relationship into a military one, because a leader who has just survived an American-backed invasion has every reason to want protection [E].

The superpowers also had motives of their own [R]. Khrushchev concluded from the failure at the Bay of Pigs that Kennedy was inexperienced and weak, and the crisis was ultimately settled by a superpower bargain in which the USA quietly removed its missiles from Turkey. Cuba was the location of the crisis, but the terms were negotiated over Castro's head between Washington and Moscow [E].

On balance Castro was a necessary but not a sufficient cause [A]. His revolution and his appeal for Soviet protection are what made Cuba available as a missile site, so the crisis could not have happened where it did without him. But he did not build the missiles, choose to send them, or decide how the confrontation ended.

The deeper point is that responsibility depends on the question being asked [A]. If we ask why the crisis happened in Cuba, Castro matters most. If we ask why it became a threat to world peace, the answer lies in a rivalry that had been building since 1945 between two powers with weapons capable of destroying the world, into which Cuba was drawn rather than which Cuba created [A].

**[10 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
> - Analysis - [A]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 10 marks require you to explain both sides and then support a valid judgement on 'how far'.
> - Explaining both sides without a supported judgement is worth 7-9 marks. Seven marks are given for one explanation on each side, with one further mark for each additional explanation on either side.
> - Explaining only one side is worth 4-6 marks, with one mark for each explanation.
> - Identifying or describing valid points without explaining them is worth 2-3 marks.
> - Writing about the topic without addressing the question is worth 1 mark.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 10 marks include:
> 
> - Narrating the Thirteen Days. The events of October 1962 are the crisis itself, not its causes, and a day-by-day account will not be credited here.
> - Writing only about the Cuban Revolution. Castro coming to power is the starting point; the question is how far he caused what followed three years later.
> - Assessing who won. That is a different question, and answering it will earn nothing here.
> - Leaving Khrushchev out entirely. The missiles were Soviet, and any judgement that ignores Soviet motives is one-sided.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Castro knew about the Bay of Pigs invasion in advance and had 20,000 soldiers ready, so his own strength contributed to the humiliation that shaped what followed.
> - Kennedy had explicitly warned Khrushchev not to place nuclear weapons on Cuba, so the decision to proceed was taken in Moscow in full knowledge of the risk.
> - The immediate trigger was American, since it was a U-2 spy plane photographing the launch pads on 14 October 1962 that turned a build-up into a crisis.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Separate the two questions hidden inside this one: why the crisis happened in Cuba, and why it became so dangerous. Castro scores heavily on the first and much less on the second, and saying so is a Level 5 judgement.
> - Use the causes framework. Long-term superpower rivalry, the medium-term effect of the Bay of Pigs and the short-term discovery of the launch pads give you a ready-made structure.
> - Dates carry the argument. February 1960 for the Soviet agreement, April 1961 for the Bay of Pigs and September 1961 for the arms pledge show the sequence by which Cuba became a Soviet base.
> - Do not treat Castro as simply a victim or simply a villain. He made real choices, but he made them in response to American pressure, and the best answers hold both together.

parts.problem_md:
The United States supported the government of South Vietnam.

Why was Diem's government unpopular in South Vietnam?
parts.solution_md:
One reason is that Diem governed against the religion of most of his people [R]. He was a Catholic in a country where Buddhists were the largest faith group, and his government discriminated against them. A ruler who treats the majority of the population as outsiders cannot expect their loyalty, and the persecution gave ordinary South Vietnamese a reason to look for an alternative to Diem rather than to defend him [E].

A second reason is that his government served itself rather than the country [R]. Diem ran a corrupt administration and handed key positions to members of his own family, so posts went to relatives rather than to able people. At the same time he took land away from peasants and gave it to rich landlords. In a country where most people farmed, reversing land reform hit the majority of the population directly in their livelihoods while a small circle around the president grew wealthier. That combination of corruption at the top and hardship at the bottom pushed many South Vietnamese towards supporting the North [E].

The result was that the National Liberation Front, formed in 1960, drew in peasants from the South as well as communists from the North, and by November 1963 the United States had withdrawn its support and Diem was overthrown and assassinated in a coup.

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 6 marks are awarded for explaining two reasons.
> - Explaining one reason is worth 4 marks, rising to 5 marks where the explanation is supported by specific contextual knowledge.
> - Identifying or describing valid reasons without explaining them is worth 2-3 marks, with one mark for each identification.
> - Writing about the topic without addressing the question is worth 1 mark.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 6 marks include:
> 
> - Explaining why the USA became involved in Vietnam. The domino theory and containment answer a different question; here the focus is Diem's standing with his own people.
> - Describing Vietcong tactics. Guerrilla warfare explains why the Vietcong were hard to beat, not why Diem was disliked.
> - Writing only that Diem was 'corrupt' or 'unpopular' without showing what he actually did. Naming the persecution of Buddhists, the appointments of family members or the transfer of land to landlords is what turns an identification into an explanation.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The Strategic Hamlets programme of 1962 was meant to shield villages from Vietcong influence but in practice destroyed homes and forced people to move, which won support for the Vietcong instead.
> - Diem refused to hold the free election promised for 1956 under the Geneva Agreement, which denied South Vietnamese people any say in who governed them.
> - Ho Chi Minh, by contrast, was widely respected and known as 'Uncle Ho', so the comparison made Diem look worse still.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Two explained reasons is the target, and religion and corruption make a strong pair because they hit different parts of the population.
> - Keep Diem himself in view. It is easy to drift into the war and lose the marks.
> - Finish each reason by saying what it made people do, such as supporting the Vietcong. That link is the difference between describing and explaining.

parts.problem_md:
The United States feared that communism would keep spreading.

What was the 'domino theory'?
parts.solution_md:
The domino theory was the American belief that if one country in a region fell to communism, the countries around it would fall one after another, like a row of dominoes toppling [1]. It was used to argue that communism had to be stopped early, even in small or distant countries that were not important to the United States in themselves [1]. President Eisenhower set the idea out publicly in 1954, when the French were losing control of Indochina [1]. It went on to become one of the main justifications for American military involvement in Vietnam [1].

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following code has been used:
> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point - [1]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point, up to a maximum of 4.
> - Four separate points are needed for four marks. Developing a point you have already made does not earn a second mark.
> - Accept all valid responses.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the Vietnam War instead of the theory. Vietnam is useful as the example the theory was used to justify, but it is not an answer on its own.
> - Confusing the domino theory with containment. Containment was the policy; the domino theory was the argument used to justify applying it in South-East Asia.
> - Judging whether the theory was correct. Evaluation earns no credit on a 4-mark recall question.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The theory assumed communism spread by outside subversion rather than by local conditions, which critics later argued was a serious misreading.
> - It was applied to South-East Asia in particular, with Laos, Cambodia and Thailand named as the dominoes that would follow Vietnam.
> - The fall of China to communism in 1949 made the idea far more persuasive to American politicians.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Start with a clear one-sentence definition, then add detail. An answer made only of examples often fails to show you understand the idea itself.
> - Keep each point in its own sentence so the examiner can count them.
> - Naming Eisenhower and 1954 is the kind of specific detail that secures the fourth mark.

Source E, written by a CIA official historian, challenges the conclusions of the Taylor Committee's official findings in Source D. However, it does not prove them wrong entirely. Source E focuses on the circumstances in which the report was written and argues that the CIA was blamed unfairly while President Kennedy was protected [S].

Both sources acknowledge that the CIA failed at the Bay of Pigs. According to Source D, the CIA failed to 'give the project appropriate organisation, staffing and full-time direction', which resulted in disaster [S]. Source D also downplays the President's role in cancelling the second air strike, arguing that better planning and timely action by the CIA could have prevented the crisis. Source E admits that 'the CIA will continue to be blamed for the failure' [S].

Source E contradicts Source D by showing that the Taylor Committee report was prepared in haste and that several important witnesses were never interviewed. The inclusion of Robert Kennedy, the President's brother, on the Committee also raises a question about its fairness [R]. Source E therefore questions how thorough the investigation was and presents it as a politically motivated exercise to protect the President's reputation. It reverses the blame, arguing that the 'actions, or inactions, of the Kennedy Administration' were responsible for the disaster [S].

To conclude, Source E does not prove that Taylor's findings were completely wrong, but it does show that they were incomplete and shaped by political interests. It undermines the reliability of Source D not by denying the CIA's failings but by exposing the bias that stopped the Committee presenting a full account. At the same time it does not overturn Source D entirely, since it agrees that the CIA will always be blamed [R].

**[8 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Source analysis - [S]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **7-8 marks:** evaluates the sources by considering the author's purpose in the context of the time, using what the author actually says.
> - **5-6 marks:** evaluates the big message of a source by cross-reference or contextual knowledge.
> - **4 marks:** evaluates details in the sources by cross-reference, contextual knowledge or purpose, without reaching the big message.
> - **3 marks:** uses everyday empathy to make something of the provenance.
> - **1-2 marks:** assertions based on provenance alone, or selects details said to be reliable or unreliable with no explanation.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 8 marks include:
> 
> - Treating it as a compare-and-contrast question. Here you must evaluate both sources and decide whether E fully disproves D, partly disproves it, or simply offers another perspective.
> - Not explaining the disagreement over who was to blame, the CIA or Kennedy's administration.
> - Stopping at the contradiction. Spotting that the two disagree is the middle of the argument, not the end.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Source D is the report of a committee that Kennedy himself appointed, so it was always likely to blame the CIA.
